title: ‘A High Potential for Abuse’: Plan to Equip ICE Agents With Electric Shock Gloves Draws Alarm From Former Officials
excerpt: Former DHS officials tell TIME that the devices aren’t necessary as an enforcement method against civilians—and that their use would pose numerous risks.
content_html:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is moving to equip immigration officers with gloves that can administer electrical shocks, a plan that is sparking alarm from former department officials.

According to a notice published by DHS this week, it will spend up to $20 million to purchase Generated Low Output Voltage Emitters, or G.L.O.V.Es, by the end of March 2027. The department, which described the gloves in the notice as a “conductive distraction and de-escalation device,” said they would be issued to Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) officers.  

“ICE is constantly assessing the needs of our officers in the field to ensure they have the tools and equipment necessary to safely arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our country,” a DHS spokesperson said in a statement to TIME.

The plan to equip immigration officers with the devices comes as the Trump Administration has faced widespread scrutiny over the use of force in its immigration crackdown, which has seen at least 10 people die in encounters with federal agents since Trump returned to office last January. 

The DHS spokesperson tells TIME that 70% of the people ICE arrests are “dangerous illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime,” echoing Trump and federal officials’ repeated claims that the crackdown is targeting the “worst of the worst”—though data have shown that a majority of those held in ICE custody during Trump’s second term have no criminal convictions on their records. 

The notice of DHS’s plans to purchase the gloves has drawn concern from former DHS officials, who tell TIME that the devices aren’t necessary as an enforcement method against the civilian population—and that their use in that capacity would pose numerous risks.

“The idea that you need tools like this, this level of force, to subdue a non-criminal immigrant who's in a secure environment … that is alarming,” says John Sandweg, who served as the acting director of ICE and acting general counsel of DHS during the Obama Administration.

Sandweg contends that there is “a high potential for abuse” with the new devices due to the rapid hiring of new immigration officers who he says are not receiving sufficient training. 

Documents produced by two DHS whistleblowers in February showed that ICE had significantly scaled up its hiring while axing several screening and training protocols for officers. 

“We're seeing lots of problems with training on use of force,” Sandweg says. He describes the plan to introduce the gloves to what he characterizes as an under-trained immigration task force that is quickly expanding as “incredibly concerning.”

The former acting ICE director argues that such a device should not be rolled out en masse, but rather “in small pilots” in order to determine that it “actually helps solve the problem” in immigration enforcement contexts and “doesn’t get abused.” 

On top of that, he contends that the device should require extensive in-person training. 

“It's tone deaf,” Sandweg says. “We’ve lost sight of the public safety mission of ICE.”

Margo Schlanger, who led DHS’s office for civil rights and civil liberties under the Obama Administration, tells TIME that a taser, which many immigration officers are equipped with or have access to, is a much more effective enforcement tool. 

And in addition to being less effective, she also argues that the gloves would pose a greater threat of harming people who have encounters with immigration officials, while making it more difficult to hold officers accountable. 

Unlike a taser, which incapacitates its target by temporarily locking up their muscles and inhibiting bodily control, the gloves “are only about pain compliance,” Schlanger says.

“They don't incapacitate. They just hurt, and so what that means is that they're not only used in a situation when a person is posing a risk to a law enforcement officer,” she says to TIME. “Pain compliance is a method of painful domination. Because of that, it's very subject to being misused. It can be used in circumstances where it's not needed. It can be used to excess.”

A taser is also more effective, safe, and humane, she contends, because it can be brandished from a distance before it is used.

“If you're actually interested in compliance, brandishing a taser is a pretty good method of eliciting compliance, and nobody gets hurt,” she says.

Schlanger references an article published by Police & Security News in which Jeff Niklaus, the founder and CEO of Compliant Technologies, which manufactures the gloves, is quoted as describing the device as “low optic”—meaning that, unlike tasers, they can be used discreetly. 

“What low optics means is that they don't want anybody watching to know that they're doing this,” Schlanger asserts. “It looks like ICE is trying to avoid public accountability. That's what this device does for them.”

Compliant Technologies declined TIME’s request for an interview. 

Jenn Rolnick Borchetta, deputy director on policing at the ACLU, similarly raises concern about this aspect of the gloves in a statement to TIME.

“They might be equipped with a device that allows them to deliver an electric shock with their hands by pushing a small button, in a move that might be imperceptible to those watching,” Borchetta says. “Giving immigration agents a concealed means of delivering terrible pain is a recipe for more harm to the public and less accountability.”

content_html_zh:
美国国土安全部 (DHS) 正在为移民官员配备可以进行电击的手套，这一计划引起了前国土安全部官员的警惕。

根据国土安全部本周发布的通知，到 2027 年 3 月底，它将花费高达 2000 万美元购买低输出电压发射器（G.L.O.V.E）。 该部门将通知中的手套描述为“传导性分散注意力和降级装置”，并表示将向移民和海关执法局（ICE）官员发放这些手套。

国土安全部发言人在给《时代》杂志的一份声明中表示：“ICE 正在不断评估我们现场官员的需求，以确保他们拥有必要的工具和设备，以安全逮捕和驱逐非法移民出境。”

为移民官员配备这些设备的计划出台之际，特朗普政府因在移民镇压中使用武力而面临广泛审查，自去年 1 月特朗普重返办公室以来，至少有 10 人在与联邦特工的冲突中死亡。

国土安全部发言人告诉《时代》杂志，ICE 逮捕的人中有 70% 是“被指控或被定罪的危险非法外国人”，这与特朗普和联邦官员一再声称的镇压行动针对的是“最坏的人”的说法相呼应——尽管数据显示，在特朗普第二任期内被 ICE 拘留的大多数人都没有刑事定罪记录。

国土安全部计划购买手套的通知引起了前国土安全部官员的担忧，他们告诉《时代》杂志，这些设备没有必要作为针对平民的执法手段，而且以这种方式使用它们会带来许多风险。

“你需要这样的工具，这种程度的武力，来制服处于安全环境中的非犯罪移民…… 这令人震惊，”奥巴马政府期间担任 ICE 代理主任和国土安全部代理总法律顾问的约翰·桑德韦格 (John Sandweg) 说道。

桑德韦格认为，由于新移民官员的快速招聘，这些新设备“很可能被滥用”，他说这些官员没有接受足够的培训。

两名国土安全部举报人二月份提供的文件显示，ICE 大幅扩大了招聘规模，同时取消了多项官员筛选和培训方案。

“我们发现使用武力的训练存在很多问题，”桑德韦格说。 他描述了将手套引入他所说的训练不足的移民特别工作组的计划，该工作组正在迅速扩大，“令人难以置信”。

这位前 ICE 代理局长认为，这样的设备不应该大规模推出，而应该“小规模试点”，以确定它在移民执法环境中“确实有助于解决问题”并且“不会被滥用”。

最重要的是，他认为该设备应该需要大量的现场培训。

“这是音盲，”桑德韦格说。 “我们忽视了 ICE 的公共安全使命。”

奥巴马政府领导下的国土安全部民权和公民自由办公室负责人玛戈·施兰格 (Margo Schlanger) 告诉《时代》杂志，许多移民官员都配备或可以使用泰瑟枪，这是一种更有效的执法工具。

她还认为，除了效果较差之外，手套还会对与移民官员接触过的人造成更大的伤害威胁，同时让追究官员责任变得更加困难。

施兰格说，与泰瑟枪不同的是，泰瑟枪会暂时锁定目标肌肉并抑制身体控制，从而使目标丧失行动能力，而手套“只关乎疼痛顺应性”。

“他们不会丧失行动能力。 它们只会造成伤害，所以这意味着它们不仅仅用于对执法人员构成风险的情况，”她对《时代》杂志说道。 “痛苦顺从是一种痛苦统治的方法。 正因为如此，它很容易被滥用。 可以在不需要的情况下使用。 它可以被过度使用。”

她认为，泰瑟枪也更有效、更安全、更人性化，因为它可以在使用前从远处挥舞。

“如果你真的对顺从感兴趣，挥舞泰瑟枪是一种很好的诱导顺从的方法，而且没有人会受伤，”她说。

施兰格引用了《警察与安全新闻》发表的一篇文章，其中引用生产手套的 Compliant Technologies 创始人兼首席执行官杰夫·尼克劳斯 (Jeff Niklaus) 的话说，该设备是“低光学”的，这意味着与泰瑟枪不同，它们可以谨慎使用。

“低光学意味着他们不希望任何人知道他们正在这样做，”施兰格断言。 “看起来 ICE 正在试图逃避公众责任。 这就是这个设备为他们做的事情。”

Compliant Technologies 拒绝了《时代》周刊的采访请求。

美国公民自由联盟 (ACLU) 治安副主任詹·罗尔尼克·博尔切塔 (Jenn Rolnick Borchetta) 在给《时代》杂志的一份声明中同样对手套的这一方面提出了担忧。

博尔切塔说：“他们可能配备了一种设备，可以让他们通过按下一个小按钮来用手施加电击，而这一举动可能被观看者察觉不到。” “给移民代理提供一种隐秘的手段来造成可怕的痛苦，只会给公众带来更多伤害，并减少责任。”
